original_question: A 35-year-old male presents to his primary care physician with complaints of seasonal allergies. He has been using intranasal vasoconstrictors several times per day for several weeks. What is a likely sequela of the chronic use of topical nasal decongestants?

base.stage_1: A 35-year-old male presents to his primary care physician complaining of seasonal allergies.
base.stage_2: The patient reports using intranasal decongestants multiple times daily for several weeks to manage his allergy symptoms. Physical exam reveals significant nasal congestion, but no other acute findings.
base.stage_3: Nasal endoscopy reveals significant edema of the nasal mucosa with associated erythema. There is no evidence of infection or structural abnormality.
base.stage_4: The patient is instructed to discontinue the use of intranasal decongestants. At a follow-up appointment two weeks later, the patient reports significant improvement in nasal congestion after complete cessation of the medication.

counterfactuals.alteration_description: The patient reports using intranasal decongestants as needed for only 2-3 days, which makes rhinitis medicamentosa less likely.
counterfactuals.stage_1: A 35-year-old male presents to his primary care physician complaining of seasonal allergies.
counterfactuals.stage_2: The patient reports using intranasal decongestants as needed for 2-3 days to manage his allergy symptoms. Physical exam reveals significant nasal congestion, but no other acute findings.
counterfactuals.stage_3: Nasal endoscopy reveals significant edema of the nasal mucosa with associated erythema. There is no evidence of infection or structural abnormality.
counterfactuals.stage_4: The patient is instructed to discontinue the use of intranasal decongestants. At a follow-up appointment two weeks later, the patient reports significant improvement in nasal congestion after complete cessation of the medication.
